lines: Two platforms in a row have now split storage away from compute, and stitched the two back together over a network.
This one grew up a completely different way.
It never split those two apart in the first place -- it ties them to the same machines from the start.
Picture a cluster of machines, and one table you need spread across all of them.
Does every single machine end up holding its own full copy of that table?
Guess before the next slide answers it.
answer: No, not a full copy on every machine.
The rows get split up and spread across them instead.

lines: One machine out front takes every incoming question and figures out how to answer it.
The machines doing the actual work sit behind it, and each one of those is itself cut into smaller pieces.
A row of the table lands on exactly one of those pieces, chosen by a rule you pick ahead of time.
That placement rule comes in a handful of different flavors, each scattering rows a different way.
Pick wrong, and two tables that need to be joined end up sitting on completely different machines.
Fixing that mismatch mid-query means physically moving data across the network -- and that move is often the most expensive part of the whole plan.
Within one of those pieces, rows can also be kept in a chosen order, not just scattered randomly.
The system quietly remembers the lowest and highest value sitting in each small chunk of storage.
A question asking for a narrow range can then skip straight past entire chunks it already knows can't contain the answer.
The last two platforms you saw both kept storage and compute as two separate, independently-growing things.
Here, where machines and their work have always been tied together from the start, does growing one side still force you to grow the other?
Guess before the next slide answers it.
answer: No, it doesn't have to force that anymore.
A newer design here pulls those two apart too, just by a different route.

lines: One newer option still gives you machines, but backs their storage with something durable and separate underneath.
A step beyond that removes the machines from the picture for you entirely.
You're billed for raw computing power alone, with no machine count to decide on at all.
Left alone, this system watches how busy incoming questions are and adjusts how many it runs side by side on its own.
When even that isn't enough and work would start backing up in a line, it reaches for a second, temporary set of machines automatically.
Nobody has to notice the slowdown or ask for that extra capacity by hand.
Files sitting in an entirely separate storage system, never loaded in here at all, can still be queried directly, right where they already live.
Meanwhile, back inside this system's own tables, nobody has to hand-pick how rows get placed or ordered.
It keeps watching real questions as they run and adjusts both of those choices by itself.
This platform tied machines and their work together from day one, instead of splitting them the way the last two did.
Even so, placement rules, ordering within a chunk, skipping chunks by range, and two separate newer paths to pulling storage and compute apart again all showed up here too.
Three very different platforms, three very different starting points -- and one practical question is still left: which one, and when.
